script.title: Stress and Anxiety Can Feel Similar but Differ
script.description: A general educational distinction from NIMH and CDC. Illustrative adults are not diagnosed participants. This is not a personal diagnosis.
script.topic: Stress and Anxiety Can Feel Similar but Differ
script.why_us: US-focused educational explanation from reviewed primary sources.
script.timely_basis: Dated historical evidence or evergreen explanation; no claim of a current trend.

scenes.narration: Stress and anxiety can share symptoms, but the National Institute of Mental Health describes an important difference.
Stress generally responds to an external cause, which can happen briefly or repeat over a longer period.

diagram.title: Stress context
diagram.note: An external demand can trigger stress.

scenes.narration: Work demands, health concerns, and relationship difficulties are examples of challenging situations described by American public health agencies.
Anxiety can occur even when no current threat is present; it is not defined only by the immediate situation.
Worry, tension, sleep disruption, or trouble concentrating can overlap, so one visible reaction does not establish a diagnosis.
The useful distinction is the context and persistence of the response, not a label assigned from somebody's photograph.

diagram.title: Similar symptoms, different context
diagram.note: General education; not a diagnosis from appearances.

sources.title: Reviewed primary-source evidence
sources.content: Stress is a physical or mental response to an external cause. A stressor can occur once, briefly, or repeatedly over time. Anxiety is a reaction to stress and can occur even without a current threat. Both can affect mind and body, with worry, tension and sleep problems among overlapping symptoms. Stress can be positive or negative, including motivation to meet a deadline or loss of sleep. These definitions are educational and do not diagnose a person.
sources.evidence_kind: editorial source summary; table rows are source data

sources.title: Reviewed primary-source evidence
sources.content: Everyone experiences occasional stress, a normal part of life. Stress is a physical and emotional response to new or challenging situations, including work, health and relationships. Stress may affect sleep, concentration and decision making. Long-term or chronic stress can worsen health problems. People respond differently; a single image or symptom does not establish a diagnosis.
